plans.hypothesis: If Darwin's claim holds, the late Chalk (latter part of the Secondary/Mesozoic) lies roughly 300 million years or more in the past, so the numeric age of the top of the Chalk-bearing Cretaceous System in the modern geological time scale is at or above about 300 Ma.
plans.pass_criterion: The International Chronostratigraphic Chart gives the top of the Cretaceous (Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, end of the Maastrichtian) an age of at least 250 Ma, so that 'far more than 300 million years since the latter part of the Secondary' is consistent with the data.
plans.fail_criterion: The chart gives the end-Cretaceous boundary an age below 150 Ma, i.e. less than half of Darwin's figure. The expected value is about 66 Ma, and the youngest Chalk (Maastrichtian) is about 72-66 Ma. Ages from 150 to 250 Ma are scored as inconclusive and as not confirming the claim.
plans.interpretation: 'Secondary period' maps to the Mesozoic Era. 'Latter part of the Secondary period / late Chalk' maps to the Upper Cretaceous (Chalk Group, about 100-66 Ma). 'Years elapsed since' maps to the numeric age in Ma of the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, the end of Chalk deposition. Darwin's denudation arithmetic is a rate-based estimate of elapsed time. The test compares it with the radiometrically and astronomically calibrated age of the boundary. It does not measure denudation itself, which is a deliberate modern reinterpretation. Fields used: unit name (Cretaceous, Upper Cretaceous, Maastrichtian) and numeric base/top ages in Ma.

dataset.name: International Chronostratigraphic Chart
dataset.why_it_fits: It is the official numeric time scale, with ages in Ma for every stage boundary, downloadable as PDF and in machine-readable form. It gives the end of the Cretaceous (about 66 Ma) and the Upper Cretaceous stages, so it can be compared with Darwin's roughly 300 Ma.

plans.hypothesis: If the claim holds, GBIF has essentially no native (non-introduced) occurrence records of Amphibia (frogs, toads, newts) on genuinely oceanic islands, though introduced populations may be recorded there.
plans.pass_criterion: From a list of at least 20 oceanic islands or archipelagos fixed in advance (for example Hawaii, Galapagos, Azores, Madeira, Canary Islands, Cape Verde, St Helena, Ascension, Tristan da Cunha, Mauritius, Reunion, Bermuda, Society Islands, Marquesas, Samoa, Tonga, Cook Islands), at least 95% have zero native amphibian species after excluding records marked INTRODUCED or INVASIVE and records with coordinate-error flags.
plans.fail_criterion: More than 10% of the pre-listed oceanic islands or archipelagos have at least one native amphibian species supported by verified, non-introduced records. A result between 5% and 10% is inconclusive.
plans.interpretation: 'Batrachians' maps to the class Amphibia (GBIF taxon key 131), including Anura and Caudata, plus caecilians as a modern addition. 'Oceanic islands' means volcanic or coral islands never joined to a continent, which excludes continental fragments such as Madagascar, the granitic Seychelles and New Zealand. 'Naturally absent' maps to no records with establishmentMeans native, or unspecified but not introduced, once errors are removed. 'Introduced frogs thrive' maps to records with establishmentMeans INTRODUCED. The sea-water mortality mechanism cannot be tested with this dataset, so only the distributional generalization is tested.

dataset.name: GBIF Occurrence Data (Amphibia, taxon key 131)
dataset.why_it_fits: The GBIF occurrence API and downloads provide taxonKey, species, country, islandGroup, island, establishmentMeans, basisOfRecord, coordinates and geospatial issue flags. These allow native versus introduced amphibian records to be counted on each pre-listed oceanic island, excluding flagged errors.
